name: Pedro Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a grader at a big open-pit gold mine, and sometimes a dozer when they're short. My job is the haul roads, keeping them smooth and properly cambered so the trucks don't wreck their tyres or slide on a wet day. A tyre on those trucks costs more than my car, so the bosses care about my roads a lot. I like that you can see your work, a road you graded at six is still there at five, and what wears me out is the dust in summer and the night shifts in winter when the cold gets into the cab.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology or AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At work the grader has GPS now, it shows me the design on a screen and tells me if I'm high or low, and after a few months I'd hate to go without it. At home I've used one of those AI chatbots a few times, once to help my daughter Sofia with a science assignment and once to write a stern letter to the council about the potholes on our street. Leila, my wife, she's a primary teacher, she uses it more than me. I'm the kind who waits till my brother-in-law has tried something first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's how it usually goes, a lot of noise and then some useful bits. I'd say the GPS on the grader was the real change and that was years ago. At work I'd joke that the robots can come and grade the road in the rain if they want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be pleased. I'm not against change, but my job's good and the pay's good and I'd like ten more years of it. If AI just helps a bit with paperwork, I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Maybe use the chatbot a bit more for the shift paperwork, the prestart forms take ages. Savings would keep going in, about one fifty a fortnight, and we'd do the trip to see Leila's family next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. Normal, like a good season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the potholes letter. Did the AI help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It made the letter more polite than I would have, which is probably why they answered it. They fixed two of the five potholes, so, partly. Leila said it sounded like a lawyer wrote it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that bothers you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the mine's already testing driverless trucks at other sites, and that's not AI hype, that's real. If trucks go driverless, someone still has to keep the roads perfect for them, maybe more perfect. So I'm not too worried, but I'd keep an eye on it.

S0.say: I'd say it's the usual story, a lot of noise and then some useful bits. The grader's GPS was the real change and that came years ago.
S0.think: I'd be pleased, because my job and pay are good and I'd like ten more years of it. If AI only helps a bit with paperwork, that suits me.
S0.do: Carries on as he is and uses the chatbot a bit more for shift paperwork. Keeps saving about one fifty a fortnight and goes ahead with the planned family trip.
S0.quote: If trucks go driverless, someone still has to keep the roads perfect for them, maybe more perfect.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is content and practical, and he thinks about technology in terms of tools he's already seen work. He separates hype from the driverless trucks he knows are real. He sees his road work as supporting automation rather than being replaced by it, at least for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we'll have to be sensible about it, workers and the company both. I wouldn't be shouting about it either way. I'd tell the guys, look, they'll still need roads, let's learn the new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think graders go automated a bit later than trucks, but they go. The GPS already does half the thinking, it's not much of a jump for it to do the steering. So I'd have a few years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on whatever new machine control they bring in, as soon as other guys say it's worth it. I'd look at the maintenance side, maybe a short course on hydraulics, because fixing the gear seems safer than driving it. And we'd bump the savings a bit, two hundred instead of one fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train once others say it's worth it. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, on the other grader. He's the type who reads every manual and tries every button. If Hamid says the course is good, I'll do it. If he says it's rubbish, I'll wait for the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's eleven, he wants to drive the big machines like his dad. I'd tell him, sure, but learn how they work inside too. A man who can only drive is in a weaker spot than a man who can fix.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big change and both workers and the company need to be sensible about it. I'd tell the guys they'll still need roads, so let's learn the new gear.
S1.think: Graders will go automated a bit later than trucks, but they will go, because GPS already does half the thinking. I'd have a few years, not forever.
S1.do: Asks for training on new machine control once colleagues vouch for it and looks at a short hydraulics course for the maintenance side. Raises savings from one fifty to two hundred a fortnight.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: A man who can only drive is in a weaker spot than a man who can fix.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro is steady: he waits for a trusted colleague, Hamid, to test things first, then follows. He thinks the grader is safe for a few years but not forever. His instinct is to move toward maintenance and he passes that to his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and I don't think anyone, company or government, is ready. I'd say we need to slow it down until there's a plan, and I'd mean it. I'm not usually one for strong views, but I'd have one on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job's gone, and the fixing job I was planning on goes too. If the robots can do hands-on work, they can fix the hydraulics as well as I can. Two years means I'd still be paying the mortgage when the pay stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all the extras: the trip to Leila's family, the new tyres on my ute I was putting off, the kids' music. I'd ask Leila how secure the school job looks, because her pay would be our base. I'd look for any job that's still hiring people, maybe road building for the council or the shire, because that might last a bit longer than the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. A sinking feeling, like the ground going soft under the grader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year timeline take away that a longer one wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choices. With ten years I could try a course, see if I like it, try another. With two, I'd grab the first thing that pays and hope. I'm a man who likes to see something work before I trust it, and there'd be no time to see anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop the kids' music. How would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia plays guitar and she'd be upset, but she's fifteen, she'd understand if we were straight with her. I'd tell her we'd start again when things settle. Daniel would just be glad to stop the recorder.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and nobody, company or government, is ready. We need to slow it down until there's a plan.
S2.think: My job is gone, and the maintenance work I was planning on goes too. Two years means I'd still be paying the mortgage when the pay stopped.
S2.do: Cuts the family trip, new ute tyres and the kids' music lessons, and relies on his wife's teaching pay as a base. Looks for jobs that may last longer, such as council road building.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a sinking feeling like the ground going soft under the grader.
S2.quote: I'm a man who likes to see something work before I trust it, and there'd be no time to see anything.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline removes Pedro's usual method of waiting for proof before acting, and that is the heart of his alarm. He takes an unusually strong view for him: slow it down. He shifts to council road work as a likely last refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to make a plan, so let's make one. Companies should tell workers early which jobs are going and when. I'd say it at work and maybe at the local meeting, but calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have three or four more good years on the grader, and then I'd need to be somewhere else. The question is where, because a robot that fixes things is in this picture too. I'd look for work with people in it, not just machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the early movers do in the first year, Hamid and the others. If someone finds a good path, I'd follow it by year two. Meanwhile we'd pay off the ute and get savings to six months, and I might do a bit of motorbike repair on weekends, which I already do for friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could still sleep. Five years feels like enough to find a path, just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the motorbike repair.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my hobby, I've got two old bikes in the garage I'm always fiddling with. Mates bring theirs round and pay me in beer, mostly. If I had to, I could charge proper money, maybe a few hundred a month, and that's something no one's building a robot for, at least I hope not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said robots would fix things too. How does that fit with the bike repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, it doesn't fit perfectly. But a bloke with an old bike wants to talk to someone about it, have a coffee, complain about parts. I think there's some work where the talking is the point. That's my hope, anyway.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but enough to make a plan. Companies should tell workers early which jobs are going and when.
S3.think: I'd have three or four more good years on the grader, then I'd need to be somewhere else. Since robots can fix things too, I'd look for work with people in it.
S3.do: Watches what early movers like Hamid do in year one and follows a proven path by year two. Pays off the ute, builds savings to six months and starts charging for weekend motorbike repairs.
S3.feel: Anxious but still sleeping, with five years feeling just about enough.
S3.quote: I think there's some work where the talking is the point.
S3.fieldNote: When gently challenged about robots fixing bikes too, Pedro admitted the gap and refined his idea toward work where conversation matters. He'd follow others rather than lead. The hobby offers him a small, real side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for things to be done properly, so let's see a proper plan from the company and the government. I'd say it's not the end of the world. That's probably how I'd put it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three, and I could probably grade roads till fifty and then do something else. The kids would be grown or nearly. So for me it's manageable, it's Daniel I'd think about more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and do the hydraulics course in the next couple of years, after Hamid. I'd build up the bike repair slowly. And Leila and I would talk to Sofia about university, maybe something in health or teaching, because she'd be starting work right about when it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the back of my mind. Like a forecast of rain next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Daniel more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he wants my job. He's eleven and he sits in the grader seat at open days and he's in heaven. In ten years there might not be a seat. I'd have to find a way to let him down gently, or find him something else to love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra time let you do that five years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let me be careful, which is how I like it. I wouldn't have to guess, I'd see what worked for other people first. And we'd have the mortgage well down, maybe a third left.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for things to be done properly, so the company and government should show a proper plan. It's not the end of the world.
S4.think: I could grade roads till about fifty and then do something else, with the kids nearly grown. It's manageable for me, and I'd worry more about my son.
S4.do: Keeps working and does a hydraulics course in the next couple of years after his colleague tries it. Grows the motorbike repair slowly and talks with his daughter about studying health or teaching.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the back of his mind, like a forecast of rain next month.
S4.quote: In ten years there might not be a seat.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Pedro can work the way he likes, carefully and after others. His worry moves from himself to his son, who dreams of the grader seat. He stays pragmatic and doesn't blame anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to see what works. What would help is someone telling us honestly, early, which jobs go when, and short courses that people have already tested, not brand new ones. Some money to bridge the gap would matter too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the roads. Everyone pictures the big trucks, but there's a lot of quiet jobs on a mine, graders, water carts, the fuel truck. We're not in the photos, but the place doesn't run without us.

headlineQuote: We're not in the photos, but the place doesn't run without us.
portrait: Pedro Farah is a 43-year-old grader operator who keeps the haul roads smooth at a large gold mine, married to a primary teacher, with two kids and a hobby fixing old motorbikes. He's careful and pragmatic, likes to see something work before he trusts it, and usually follows a keen colleague, Hamid, rather than going first. He stays calm or uneasy in the slower pictures and becomes alarmed only when two-year AGI removes the time to watch and learn. With more warning he'd move toward maintenance and small bike repairs, while worrying about his son who dreams of the grader seat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to see what works before choosing a path.
whatWouldHelp: Honest, early notice of which jobs go when, short courses that others have already tested, and money to bridge the gap.
